blocks.text: Quick verdict

SOAX is the stronger network for mobile-heavy, ad-verification and multi-country work: it is several times larger, puts mobile and residential on one rate, supports UDP and QUIC, and its Tier 3 country prices undercut Infatica. Infatica is the better choice for US-focused work at small volumes ($40 for 10 GB against $50 on SOAX Sandbox), for ZIP targeting without a Scale plan, and for buyers who prefer subscriptions without 60-day credit expiry. Compliance teams will find Infatica's sourcing disclosures more detailed.

SOAX and Infatica both sell residential and mobile proxies with fine-grained targeting, and both are popular with ad-verification and market-research teams. SOAX is the bigger network, with 155M residential and 33M mobile IPs on one balance and UDP and QUIC support, but its credits expire and its rate depends on the exit country. Infatica uses familiar per-GB subscriptions, includes ZIP targeting on every plan and emphasises ethical sourcing. This comparison weighs scale and protocols against simplicity and precision.

blocks.text: SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX is a residential and mobile specialist known for granular filtering. Its 2026 pricing replaced fixed GB bundles with plans (Sandbox, Builder, Team, Scale, Enterprise) that include credits, and the credit burn rate depends on the exit country's tier. That makes SOAX cheap for some geographies and expensive for low-volume US work. The network is large (155M residential, 33M mobile advertised) and supports protocols few competitors offer, including UDP and QUIC.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica pitches itself on ethical sourcing and features available to every customer. All residential plans include country, city and ZIP targeting, IP whitelisting and selectable rotation times, and a 7-day $4 trial lowers the risk of testing. Independent reviewers have found its proxies fast and its pool modest but respectable. Its niche extra is a premium IPv6 residential pool, rare in this market, at about 1.5x the normal per-GB price.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Pricing: SOAX vs Infatica

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $40 with Infatica and $50 with SOAX: a 20% saving in Infatica's favour. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $300 with SOAX and $360 with Infatica: a 17% saving in SOAX's favour. Both SOAX and Infatica work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

SOAX has the bigger advertised network, 155M residential + 33M mobile residential IPs against 35M-40M for Infatica, roughly 4.4 times larger. Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, SOAX lists 195 countries and Infatica lists 195. On targeting, SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans, while Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes, and Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With SOAX: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging. With Infatica: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests. Run the same small test on both before committing.

SERP and rank tracking: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With SOAX: city and ISP targeting for local results. With Infatica: ZIP targeting helps local search results. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Social media and multi-account management: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. How Infatica compares: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. SOAX: granular location filters. Infatica: ZIP-level targeting for local prices. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Ad verification and geo-testing: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. How Infatica compares: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing.

Tight budgets: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With SOAX: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs. With Infatica: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Verification and payment rules differ too. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test SOAX and Infatica before you commit
The quickest way to choose between SOAX and Infatica is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99; Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile)).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, SOAX comes out ahead in 2, Infatica in 0, and 4 are ties. That makes SOAX the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms, while Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
